'''''Poa pratensis''''', commonly known as '''Kentucky bluegrass''' (or '''blue grass'''), '''smooth meadow-grass''', or '''common meadow-grass''', is a [[perennial]] species of [[Poaceae|grass]] native to practically all of [[Europe]], [[North Asia]] and the mountains of [[Algeria]], [[Morocco]], and [[Tunisia]]. There is disagreement about its native status in [[North America]], with some sources considering it native<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gleason |first=Henry A. (Henry Allan) |url=https://archive.org/details/manualofvascular0000glea |title=Manual of vascular plants of northeastern United States and adjacent Canada |date=1991 |location=The Bronx, N.Y. |publisher=New York Botanical Garden |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-89327-365-1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Poa Pratensis |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=POPR |access-date=September 10, 2024 |website=University of Texas Ladybird Johnson Wildflower Center}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Element Stewardship Abstract for Poa pratensis, Poa compressa Kentucky Bluegrass, Canada Bluegrass |url=https://www.invasive.org/gist/esadocs/documnts/poa_pra.pdf |access-date=September 10, 2024 |website=www.invasives.org}}</ref> and others stating the [[Spanish Empire]] brought the seeds of Kentucky bluegrass to the [[New World]] in mixtures with other grasses.<ref>{{cite web |author=Martin Anderson, Texas AgriLife Extension Service |title=Kentucky Bluegrass |url=http://aggie-horticulture.tamu.edu/archives/parsons/turf/publications/Bluegrass.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230508211011/https://soilcrop.tamu.edu/program/turfgrass/ |archive-date=2023-05-08 |publisher=Aggie Horticulture}}</ref> It is a very popular lawn grass in North America with the species being spread over all of the cool, humid parts of the [[United States]]. In its native range, ''Poa pratensis'' forms a valuable pasture plant, characteristic of well-drained, fertile soil. It is also used for making [[lawn]]s in [[Park|parks]] and [[Garden|gardens]] and has established itself as a common [[Invasive species|invasive]] weed across cool moist [[Temperate climate|temperate climates]] like the [[Pacific Northwest]] and the [[Northeastern United States]]. When found on native [[grassland]]s in [[Canada]], for example, it is considered an unwelcome [[exotic plant]], and is indicative of a disturbed and degraded landscape.<ref>{{cite web |author=Ksenija Vujnovic |author2=Ross W. Wein |date=September 1997 |title=An Inventory of Remnant Prairie Grasslands Within the Central Parkland Natural Sub-Region of Alberta |url=https://www.albertaparks.ca/media/3195225/parkland_report_remnant_prairie.pdf |page=5}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-03-15 |title=There Are More Than a Dozen Types of Grass — Here's How to Know Which One You Have |url=https://www.popularmechanics.com/home/lawn-garden/a32130743/types-of-grass/ |access-date=2023-08-31 |website=Popular Mechanics |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Poa pratensis'' was one of the many species described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his landmark work ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' in 1753. {{transliteration|grc|Poa}} is [[Ancient Greek language|Greek]] for [[fodder]] and ''pratensis'' is derived from {{lang|la|pratum}}, [[Latin]] for [[meadow]]. The name Kentucky bluegrass derives from its flower heads, which are blue when the plant is allowed to grow to its natural height of {{convert|2|to|3|ft|cm|-1|abbr=in|order=flip}}.<ref>{{cite news |last=Ryen |first=Dag |date=June 3, 1993 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/06/03/opinion/l-what-makes-kentucky-s-bluegrass-blue-528593.html |title=What Makes Kentucky's Bluegrass Blue |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |page=22 |access-date=2018-06-15}}</ref>

''Poa pratensis'' is the [[type (botany)|type species]] of the grass family [[Poaceae]].

Five subspecies are accepted.<ref name = powo>{{cite web |title=''Poa pratensis'' L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:417792-1 |website=[[Plants of the World Online]] |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |access-date=10 February 2025}}</ref>
*''Poa pratensis'' subsp. ''dolichophylla'' {{small|(Hack.) Portal}} – Corsica
*''Poa pratensis'' subsp. ''jordanii'' {{small|Portal}} – eastern France
*''Poa pratensis'' subsp. ''oligantha'' {{small|Charit.}} – western Siberia
*''Poa pratensis'' subsp. ''pratensis'' – temperate North America and Eurasia; Yemen, the Philippines, Java, and New Guinea
*''Poa pratensis'' subsp. ''turfosa'' {{small|(Litv.) Vorosch.}} – Baltic States and northern and Central European Russia

==Description==
''Poa pratensis'' is a [[herbaceous]] perennial plant {{convert|30|–|70|cm}} tall. The [[leaf|leaves]] have boat-shaped tips, narrowly linear, up to {{convert|20|cm|sigfig=1}} long and {{convert|3|–|5|mm}} broad, smooth or slightly roughened, with a rounded to truncate ligule {{convert|1|–|2|mm}} long. The conical [[panicle]] is {{convert|5|–|20|cm|sigfig=1}} long, with 3 to 5 branches in the basal whorls; the oval [[spikelet]]s are {{convert|3|–|6|mm}} long with 2 to 5 [[floret]]s, and are purplish-green or grey. They are in flower from May to July, compared to annual meadowgrass (''[[Poa annua]]'') which is in flower for eight months of the year. ''Poa pratensis'' has a fairly prominent mid-vein (center of the blade).

The [[ligule]] is extremely short and square-ended, making a contrast with annual meadowgrass (''[[Poa annua]]'') and rough meadowgrass (''[[Poa trivialis]]'') in which it is silvery and pointed. The Kentucky bluegrass is a dark green/blue compared to the apple-green color of ''Poa annua'' and ''Poa trivialis''.

The [[rootstock]] is creeping, with runners ([[rhizome]]s). The broad, blunt leaves tend to spread at the base, forming close mats.

==Ecology==
[[File:PP Na Popovickem kopci 007 cf Myrmus miriformis.jpg|thumb|''[[Myrmus]] miriformis'' in [[Přerov]], Czech Republic]]
''Poa pratensis'' is among the food plants of the caterpillars of the meadow brown (''[[Meadow brown|Maniola jurtina]]''), gatekeeper (''[[Gatekeeper (butterfly)|Pyronia tithonus]]''), and [[pepper-and-salt skipper]] butterflies; the common sun beetle (''[[Amara aenea]]'') (adults feed on the developing seeds), the [[leafhopper]] ''[[Eupelix cuspidata]]'', the grassbug ''[[Myrmus miriformis]]'' (feeds on young blades and developing seeds),<ref>[http://www.plantpress.com/wildlife/o1084-roughmeadowgrass.php Natural England description on website] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090223215305/http://www.plantpress.com/wildlife/o1084-roughmeadowgrass.php|date=2009-02-23}}</ref> and the club-horned grasshopper (''[[Aeropedellus clavatus]]'') (feeds on the blades, seeds, and glumes).<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Pfadt |first=Robert E. |date=1994 |title=Species Fact Sheet - Clubhorned Grasshopper |url=https://www.ars.usda.gov/ARSUserFiles/30320505/grasshopper/Extras/PDFs/Species%20Fact%20Sheets/Clubhorn.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241208181511/https://www.ars.usda.gov/ARSUserFiles/30320505/grasshopper/Extras/PDFs/Species%20Fact%20Sheets/Clubhorn.pdf |archive-date=2024-12-08 |access-date=2025-01-29 |website=Wyoming Agricultural Experiment Station Bulletin 912 · Grasshopper Species Fact Sheets |publisher=Agricultural Research Service U.S. Department of Agriculture - Pest Management Research: Sidney, MT}}</ref>

''Poa pratensis'' is host to a number of [[fungi]], including ''[[Claviceps purpurea]]'', which causes [[ergotism]] when consumed, ''[[Drechslera poae]]'', ''[[Epichloë typhina]]'', ''[[Phaeoseptoria poae]]'', ''[[Puccinia brachypodii]]'' var. ''poae-nemoralis'', ''[[Stagonospora montagnei]]'', ''[[Stagonospora nodorum]]'' and ''[[Wojnowicia hirta]]''.<ref Name="HH&GGE2004">Helgi Hallgrímsson & Guðríður Gyða Eyjólfsdóttir (2004). [https://rafhladan.is/bitstream/handle/10802/4090/Fjolrit_45.pdf?sequence=1 ''Íslenskt sveppatal I - smásveppir'' [Checklist of Icelandic Fungi I - Microfungi]. Fjölrit Náttúrufræðistofnunar. Náttúrufræðistofnun Íslands [Icelandic Institute of Natural History]. ISSN 1027-832X</ref>

==Cultivation and production==
The [[Central Kentucky Blue Grass Seed Company Building]] is on the National Register of Historic Places. Since the 1950s and early 1960s, 90% of Kentucky bluegrass seed in the United States has been produced on specialist farms in [[Idaho]], [[Oregon]] and [[Washington (state)|Washington]].

During the 1990s,{{citation needed|date=March 2022}} botanists began experimenting with hybrids of ''Poa pratensis'' and Texas bluegrass (''[[Poa arachnifera|P. arachnifera]]''), with the goal of creating a [[drought]] and heat-resistant lawn grass. In warm climates, such hybrids may remain green year-round.<ref name="KSU">{{cite web | title=Texas Bluegrass Hybrids – Bluegrass Research – Research – Bremer – Turf Information | website=[[Kansas State University Research and Extension]] | date=2004-11-04 | url=http://www.k-state.edu/turf/bremer/research/bluegrass/hybrid-bluegrass/ | access-date=2022-03-19}}</ref>

Bella Bluegrass is a brand-named dwarf variant of ''Poa pratentis'' developed by the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]]. It has relatively deep roots and propagates relatively rapidly horizontally from its root system but grows to only {{convert|2|-|5|in|cm|0}} in above-ground height, basically eliminating the need for [[mowing]] lawns that use it. It cannot be reproduced by seed and thus depends on [[Plug (horticulture)|sod plugs]] or [[sprigging]] for its production.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gardeningknowhow.com/lawn-care/specific/kentucky-bluegrass/bella-grass-information.htm |title=What Is Bella Grass: Information On No Mow Bella Turf Grass |last=Grant |first=Bonnie L. |website=Gardening Know-How |date=15 February 2023 |access-date=2023-02-21}}</ref>
